evidence.label: No bigeodesics in planar first-passage percolation
Strict convexity and differentiability of the planar exponential first-passage limit shape

headline: Planar random-metric grids are claimed to have no route that is fastest forever both ways, and a smooth limit shape.
scope: First-passage percolation on the square grid: iid nonatomic weights with a moment condition for bigeodesics; exponential and Gamma weights for the shape.
plain: Give each road of a square grid a random travel time and measure distance by the fastest route. One paper claims that no route is fastest forever in both directions, under a mild moment condition. The other studies the large-scale shape of the reachable region. For exponential travel times it claims the shape has no flat edges and no corners. Lean has a formal proof of the no-corners part, for every Gamma law.
doesNot: This does not give a formula for the limit shape, or remove the moment condition from the no-bigeodesics result.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: John Hammersley and Dominic Welsh, first-passage percolation
scorecard.significanceWhy: It would settle two long-standing planar conjectures, one of them with a partial Lean proof.

explanation:
Picture a square grid of roads. Each road segment has its own random travel time. Take one small square of four segments. Going right then up costs 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9 hours. Going up then right costs 0.2 + 0.9 = 1.1 hours. So the fastest time between opposite corners is 0.9 hours, along the first route. This is first-passage percolation: a random grid whose distance is the fastest travel time[1]. A fastest route is called a geodesic.

Now make the grid infinite. Over long distances, travel time grows in proportion to the distance, but at different rates in different directions. The set of points reachable within time t, shrunk by a factor of t, settles into a fixed convex shape[2]. This is the limit shape. Its exact form is unknown even for simple weights. For exponential travel times, its fine geometry was a long-open question[3].

Two papers address this setting. The first asks about routes that are fastest in both directions forever. Such a route is called a bigeodesic. The question goes back to Furstenberg, as recorded by Kesten[4]. The conjecture says that, for continuous random weights, no bigeodesic exists[5]. The first paper claims to prove this, with one condition[6]. The smallest of four independent weights must have finite average square[6]. It rules out all bigeodesics at once, with no assumption on the limit shape[7].

The second paper looks at the limit shape itself, for exponential weights. Two things could make the shape irregular. A flat edge is a straight piece of boundary. A corner is a point where the boundary has more than one tangent line[8]. The paper claims the shape has neither: it is strictly convex and its boundary is smooth, a C¹ curve[9]. It also proves smoothness for every Gamma law of weights, a wider family that includes the exponential[10].

Earlier results came with assumptions. Newman showed that routes have directions, but needed curvature of the shape and an extra moment condition[11]. Damron and Hanson excluded some bigeodesics, but needed the shape to be smooth in places[12]. Licea and Newman excluded bigeodesics only for directions chosen in advance[13]. The single obstacle was that every method needed some regularity of the unknown shape. The first paper removes that need. Its argument handles every possible direction at once.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof that the shape's boundary is smooth. It covers every Gamma law of weights, including the exponential one. Strict convexity of the exponential shape lies outside that check. So does the absence of bigeodesics. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Smoothness of the shape for Gamma weights has a Lean proof; strict convexity and the no-bigeodesics result do not. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A grid with random travel times on its edges, where distance is the fastest total travel time.
A fastest route between two points.
A path, infinite in both directions, every piece of which is a fastest route.
The convex shape that the region reachable within time t approaches after shrinking by t.
Having no straight pieces on the boundary.
A boundary with a single tangent line at every point, so no corners.
A family of probability laws for positive numbers that includes the exponential law.
